concept.name: Ontology
concept.definition: In computer and information science, an explicit specification of a conceptualization: a set of representational primitives — classes, attributes, and relations — with definitions of their meaning and constraints on their logically consistent use, used to model a domain of knowledge (Gruber). Ontologies sit at the 'semantic' level, above logical and physical data models, and enable interoperability and automated reasoning.
concept.intuition: A formal contract about what kinds of things exist in a domain and how they may relate, so that different systems and people use the same words to mean the same things.
concept.mechanics: An ontology defines classes (e.g., Derivative), properties (e.g., hasUnderlying), hierarchies (subclass relations), and constraints (e.g., every futures contract has exactly one expiry), typically expressed in formalisms such as OWL whose expressive power approaches first-order logic. Systems commit to the ontology by making assertions consistent with its definitions and constraints.
concept.failure_modes: Over-rigid ontologies break when the domain evolves or crosses boundaries (hybrid instruments, novel asset classes); over-permissive ones degenerate into unstructured glossaries. Mismatched ontologies across systems recreate the interoperability problem they were meant to solve.
concept.misconceptions: An ontology is not merely a list of terms or a folder hierarchy — without formal relations and constraints it is a taxonomy or glossary at best. It also specifies a vocabulary, not a database of facts about individuals.
concept.example: A trading ontology declares that Option is a subclass of Derivative with mandatory properties underlyingAsset, strike, and expiry, so any system exchanging option data validates records against the same conceptual model.

citations.source: Gruber, T., 'Ontology' (entry in Encyclopedia of Database Systems, Springer; update of the 1993 definition)
